content.text: Why does a small piece of lead feel heavy while a large piece of wood feels light? The answer lies in density—a property that tells us how much mass is packed into a given volume. Understanding density helps explain floating, sinking, and many other everyday phenomena.
Density measures how much mass is contained in a given volume. It is calculated using the equation density = mass / volume (rho = m / V) and is measured in kg/m cubed or g/cm cubed.
is the mass per unit volume of a substance.
It tells us how "concentrated" the mass is
Density is an intrinsic property (doesn't depend on the size of the sample)
Different states have different densities (solid ≈ liquid >> gas)

Students sometimes confuse mass and density. A large object can have a low density (e.g., a big block of foam), while a small object can have a high density (e.g., a lead weight). Density depends on both mass and volume.
An object floats in a fluid if its density is less than the density of the fluid. An object sinks if its density is greater than the fluid's density.
Ice floats on water (ice density 920 kg/m³ < water density 1000 kg/m³)
A steel ship floats because the average density (including air inside) is less than water
Helium balloons rise because helium is less dense than air

Ships are designed with large volumes of air inside. The average density (steel + air) is less than water, so they float.
Hot air is less dense than cold air. The balloon rises because the total density is less than the surrounding air.
Submarines control their density by filling or emptying ballast tanks with water. More water = higher density = sink; less water = lower density = rise.
Oil floats on water because oil is less dense. This is used in cooking and salad dressings.
— It's not about weight; it's about density. A heavy cruise ship floats because its average density is less than water.
"Steel sinks, so steel ships should sink"
— The ship includes air, giving it a lower average density.
— Density is mass per unit volume. A large object can have more mass but lower density than a small object.
"All solids are denser than all liquids"
— Not true. Cork (solid) is less dense than water (liquid).
— Ice is actually less dense than water, which is why it floats.
